chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
title: Auditioning for Eddie Heywood Sr. with Butterbeans and Susie
summary: Heywood Sr. needs a trombone for the TOBA show at the Dixie Theatre; Fields reads the book, the band tests him with a jam, and Heywood hires him.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: I would just like to mention something before--that's just the beginning of my first being around a band, but a very important thing I'd like to say, while I was doing the gig with Ball and the gig with Thomas it was getting around that there was some youngster in town that plays a pretty good trombone. So, Butterbeans and Susie came to town and Eddie
Heyward Sr. was in charge of the band, and he wanted to augment the band. He was going to be in the Dixie Theatre for two weeks and this is on the TOBA*circuit--

So somebody told him--I think the man that ran the theatre--he asked what he wanted, and he said well, I want a trumpet and I would like to have a trombone for this gig in here, and he said there's this younster around here who plays. By coincidence, the theatre was only about a half a block from the

electric shop where I was working, and they had told him that he works down there at this electric shop. So he made it his business one morning to come down and talk to me and said that he'd like me to work with him, and I told him yes, I'd be glad to. He said--he was kind of nice--he said, first, do you read? And I said yes, fairly. He said we'd have to have a rehearsal before I could just tell you it's your job. I said okay; when? From the beginning, I don't know why, the bosses were very nice to me and when they found out I was playing, he said well, anytime you want, but your time don't go with you then. I said that's all right.
So I went to rehearsal with Eddie, and the first thing they did was (inaudible) and everybody was just smiling. They were surprised. So they threw out the finale and everybody was grinning--
I think that you were very young and you did well.

tickled to death. Finally--which I learned later from experience--they were all happy over me, but this trumpet player that was sitting next to, I think--I know, because he saw I was reading it to a tee but (inaudible), and he said let's jam a little, and Eddie said, you're the very one who didn't want to rehearse, and here's this man that came here and played the hardest stuff we have in the book, what do you want to bother him for, let him go back to his job, the man has a job. You didn't want to rehearse anyway. So this trumpet player gave a kind of wink to the drummer--I never will forget it--and that was the introduction that this drummer had the same number that they were playing and rolled off and then all of them fell in and of course I caught on, and so (inaudible) said to me, take one and I went on with my trombone and Eddie Heyward turned around and he stuttered-- if you know him or ever met him, because his son

does too, but he stutters very bad and he goes ba-ba-ba-ba-I never seen nobody play that much music and play a damn thing; but I'm going to take you, you got a job. He said I got a son just about your age, you got the foundation, I'm going to make a musician out of you. He said how in the world did you read all that music and can't play nothing. So I said I haven't been doing anything like that. Well, that's all right, I'm going to carry you with me.
Do you remember the number that they were jamming?
I don't remember. Anyway, to tell you the truth, I never did amount to anything as far as jamming.
The men, frankly speaking, just relived that whole time (inaudible), and you know what you can do and it's all right, and of course they would allow (inaudible).
